name: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 13 (KCNC3)
aliases: autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type SCA13

clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant ataxia caused by missense variants in KCNC3, which encodes the Kv3.3 voltage-gated potassium channel needed for high-frequency firing of cerebellar neurons, making it a channelopathy rather than a repeat-expansion disorder

Two broad phenotypes are recognised: an infantile or childhood-onset form with motor developmental delay, intellectual disability and often relatively stable ataxia, and a later adult-onset progressive cerebellar ataxia
Core features include gait and limb ataxia, dysarthria and nystagmus, with cognitive impairment prominent in the early-onset form and pyramidal signs in some
Particular KCNC3 variants tend to correlate with the early-onset versus adult-onset phenotype, reflecting distinct effects on channel gating
Because the causative changes are point mutations, repeat-expansion assays are normal and diagnosis requires gene sequencing by panel or exome
Brain MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, and in early-onset cases cerebellar hypoplasia may be present
Management is supportive; there is no therapy that corrects the underlying channel defect
reference.pathophysiology: SCA13 arises from heterozygous missense variants in KCNC3, encoding the Kv3.3 voltage-gated potassium channel that enables rapid repolarisation and sustained high-frequency firing in Purkinje cells and deep cerebellar and brainstem neurons. The mutations alter channel gating, acting through loss of function or dominant-negative effects, which impairs the precise, fast firing these neurons depend upon. In developmental (early-onset) variants this disturbance additionally affects cerebellar development, so the phenotype can combine neurodevelopmental impairment with cerebellar dysfunction, whereas adult-onset variants tend to cause progressive Purkinje cell degeneration and ataxia.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital cerebellar hypoplasia and other early-onset developmental ataxias
Other channelopathy ataxias such as episodic ataxia types 1 and 2
Cerebral palsy in children presenting with delay and ataxia
additionalInvestigations: KCNC3 sequencing as part of an ataxia gene panel or exome
Brain MRI to characterise cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia
Testing for common repeat-expansion SCAs to exclude commoner causes
Developmental and neuropsychological assessment in children with delay
Detailed family history to establish autosomal dominant transmission
Screening for metabolic and acquired ataxia causes where the presentation is atypical
redFlags: Developmental regression or rapid progression suggesting an alternative or acquired disorder
Seizures pointing to a broader neurodevelopmental or metabolic process
Severe bulbar dysfunction with feeding difficulty or aspiration, particularly in infants
New focal neurological signs indicating a structural lesion
reference.prognosis: In the early-onset form disability is often relatively static but combined with lasting developmental and cognitive impact, whereas the adult-onset form is slowly progressive; overall course and severity vary with the specific variant, and many patients retain useful mobility for extended periods.
pitfalls: Expecting a repeat expansion and missing the point mutation when panels for common SCAs are negative
Mislabelling an early-onset child as having cerebral palsy rather than a genetic ataxia
Not proceeding to gene sequencing, which is required to detect KCNC3 variants
Overlooking the developmental phenotype and its implications for schooling and support
Failing to provide genetic counselling given dominant inheritance and variable expressivity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide symptomatic and supportive care, as no disease-modifying therapy exists for this Kv3.3 potassium-channel disorder
Maintain function with physiotherapy, occupational therapy, gait aids and speech and language therapy for dysarthria
Provide developmental support, special educational input and neuropsychological care in the early-onset form with intellectual disability
Treat associated pyramidal signs and manage swallowing safety as bulbar features develop
Monitor the course, which is often static in early-onset disease and slowly progressive in the adult-onset form
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and predictive or cascade gene testing
